strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: identifies the performance gap of cross-attention VLMs on fine-grained visual tasks and links it to the lack of text-to-text interaction.
Simple, modular CASA mechanism with multiple variants (CASA→, CASA⊕, CASA∨) that can be integrated into existing VLMs with modest parameter overhead.
Extensive empirical validation: controlled comparisons from a text-only LLM and adaptation of Qwen2.5-VL, across document/chart understanding, OCR, general VQA, and video benchmarks.
Strong ablations: CASA vs. vanilla/gated cross-attention, placement of CASA layers, token compression, FFN updates, and masking self-attention support the main design choices.
Practical efficiency analysis and streaming video captioning demonstrate low memory growth and latency, a genuine advantage over token insertion for long/streaming contexts.
Good reproducibility: public datasets, detailed training setup, lmms-eval evaluation, and released code/models promised.
weaknesses: Performance gap to token insertion is reduced but not closed, especially on fine-grained tasks such as InfoVQA, ChartQA, AI2D, and MME; the abstract/intro wording 'largely closes' overstates the evidence.
Novelty is incremental: CASA mainly augments cross-attention by including text tokens as keys/values; the core insight is empirical rather than deeply architectural.
Evidence for 'implicit gating' is indirect; masking self-attention at inference shows reliance on self-attention but does not directly establish softmax-based gating as the mechanism.

Some efficiency and comparison claims are not fully apples-to-apples: insertion baselines often train with shorter sequences/lower resolution due to memory, while CASA trains at higher resolution, and CASA⊕ training is slower than insertion in Table 1.

Streaming evaluation relies on LLM-as-judge win rates against LiveCC; quantitative memory/latency plots are helpful, but the final win rate remains below 7B LiveCC, so streaming superiority is not unambiguous.
The paper lacks a dedicated limitations/societal-impact discussion, and potential biases in the public training data are not addressed.

strengths: The paper introduces CASA, a simple and modular fusion mechanism that adds local text-to-text interaction inside cross-attention layers, with three variants (CASA^→, CASA^⊕, CASA^∨) and controlled ablations.
It provides a broad empirical study: training from a text-only LLM, adapting a pretrained Qwen2.5-VL model, image benchmarks, video benchmarks, and streaming video captioning.
The ablation in Table 8 and attention visualization in Appendix A make a plausible case that self-attention in CASA layers is important for performance.
The efficiency analysis and streaming memory/latency measurements highlight practical advantages of cross-attention-style fusion, and the paper appears to release code/models and use public datasets.
weaknesses: The central claim that CASA 'largely closes the gap' to token insertion is overstated. In Table 2, CASA from scratch still drops about 7% on average and much more on fine-grained tasks (e.g., InfoVQA 48.6 vs. 61.8, ChartQA 73.4 vs. 81.6). In Table 3, adapting Qwen2.5-VL still loses about 5% on average, with large drops on InfoVQA (59.6 vs. 71.6), MME (1918 vs. 2249), and AI2D (75.1 vs. 80.1). These are precisely the fine-grained tasks used to motivate the work, so the main problem is not solved convincingly.

The local-window design prevents text tokens after a new image from attending to earlier images (Equation 3 and Section 3.2). This is a serious limitation for multi-image/interleaved conversations, yet the abstract and contributions claim scalability for 'long-context multimodal tasks' and 'long interleaved image-text sequences' without evaluating any multi-image or interleaved image-text benchmark. Standard cross-attention and token insertion can attend to all previous image tokens; CASA cannot, and this limitation is not discussed or tested.

The cross-attention baselines in Table 6 are suspiciously weak compared to published mPLUG-Owl3 numbers (e.g., HRES 30 vs. 48.5 ChartQA in Table 2), suggesting the in-house cross-attention baseline may be undertrained or poorly tuned. This inflates CASA's apparent advantage. The token-insertion baseline also uses lower resolution and shorter sequences due to memory constraints, confounding both performance and efficiency comparisons (Tables 1 and 2).

Efficiency claims are not fully supported. Table 1 shows CASA^⊕ training time (10h14) is not meaningfully better than token insertion (10h29), even though insertion used reduced sequence lengths and lower resolution. Table 11 reports inference total time +6% for CASA^⊕ and only ~14% memory reduction. The main efficiency gain comes from not passing image tokens through FFNs, which standard cross-attention also does; CASA's efficiency advantage over cross-attention itself is therefore unclear.

The streaming video captioning results are weaker than claimed: CASA 3B reaches 39.4 winrate vs. LiveCC-7B-Base 43.2 and LiveCC-7B-Instruct 41.5 (Table 9). Calling these scores 'similar' overstates the result, and there are no error bars or human evaluations to assess reliability of the LLM-as-judge metric.

The methodological novelty is incremental: CASA is essentially cross-attention with text tokens concatenated as keys/values inside local attention windows. The 'implicit gating' effect is just the softmax balancing text and image keys, which is closely related to existing gated cross-attention designs. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish CASA from simply adding text tokens to a cross-attention KV or from other gated fusion variants.

The paper lacks a meaningful limitations section, failure-case analysis, or societal-impact discussion. It does not analyze when CASA's local windows hurt, how CASA^∨ affects global text attention, or what happens with many images over long conversations. Some formatting and typos also reduce clarity (e.g., shifted Table 2 row and 'mPhig-Owl3').

Reproducibility details are incomplete: while inference code and models are promised, the exact initialization/projection of image tokens in CASA layers and training code are not fully specified, making independent reproduction harder.

strengths: The paper identifies a clear and important limitation of cross-attention-based VLMs: text tokens do not interact with each other during visual knowledge injection, which is convincingly linked to poor fine-grained visual understanding.

CASA is a simple, modular, and well-motivated modification of cross-attention that preserves its efficiency advantages: image tokens are not inserted into the KV cache or passed through the LLM's FFNs, making it attractive for streaming and long-context multimodal applications.

The experimental evaluation is broad and strong: it includes training from a text-only LLM, adapting a frozen pretrained VLM, image and video benchmarks, live video captioning, and controlled ablations.

The ablations on the self-attention component are persuasive, especially the inference-time masking study and attention-score visualization, which support the claim that text-to-text interaction provides an implicit gating effect.
The efficiency analyses and streaming captioning results demonstrate practical benefits over token insertion in memory usage and latency, which is a valuable contribution beyond benchmark accuracy.
Reproducibility is reasonably well supported through use of public datasets, detailed training configurations, lmms-eval evaluation, and a project page with code/models.
weaknesses: The method does not fully close the gap to token insertion. Consistent drops remain on high-resolution document/chart understanding (e.g., InfoVQA, ChartQA, DocVQA) and when adapting Qwen2.5-VL, so claims such as 'on par' or 'largely closes' should be qualified.

The comparison with token insertion is not fully apples-to-apples: the insertion baseline is trained at lower resolution and shorter sequences because of memory limits, while CASA is trained at higher resolution and longer sequences. This may disadvantage insertion and should be discussed more carefully.

The controlled cross-attention baselines perform surprisingly poorly on high-resolution tasks compared to published mPLUG-Owl3 numbers, suggesting possible configuration or training sensitivity. A clearer explanation of this discrepancy would strengthen the claims.

The streaming video captioning comparison is promising but incomplete: the main quantitative table compares mainly to LiveCC-7B, while a direct, controlled insertion-based baseline of comparable size is not shown in the main paper.
The 'implicit gating' mechanism is supported mainly by ablations and attention statistics rather than a formal analysis, so the interpretation remains plausible but not fully established.

The CASA variants add architectural complexity, especially CASA^V replacing self-attention layers with local attention, which may limit global text coherence. The placement study helps, but this trade-off deserves more discussion.

strengths: The paper provides a clear and systematic decomposition of cross-attention versus token insertion into five key differences (D1-D5), which helps structure the performance-efficiency trade-offs and makes the empirical findings more interpretable.

The controlled image experiments are a strength: the same training data, backbone, and pipeline are used for both cross-attention and token-insertion variants, allowing a fairer comparison than much of the prior literature.

The adaptation of a strong pretrained insertion-based VLM (Qwen2.5-VL-3B) to cross-attention demonstrates that a simple CA adaptation can retain most base-model performance while gaining efficiency benefits, and can outperform previous CA-based VLMs of larger size on several benchmarks.

The streaming video captioning application provides compelling practical evidence: CA maintains near-constant memory and low latency over long horizons, whereas token-insertion models rapidly increase memory and slow down.
The paper is generally well written, with informative figures and tables, and provides substantial implementation/training details. Releasing code and models supports reproducibility.
Ablations on layer frequency, token compression, FFN updates, and image resolution add useful practical guidance for practitioners choosing between fusion mechanisms.
weaknesses: The core contribution is primarily an empirical re-evaluation and simple variant study rather than a new algorithmic mechanism. The main method is vanilla cross-attention with lightweight modifications, so the technical novelty is limited relative to typical ECCV algorithm papers.

A significant performance gap remains on high-resolution document, chart, and infographic understanding tasks. The paper identifies likely causes such as lack of image-token updates and no explicit multi-image history, but does not propose a convincing way to close this gap.

The live video captioning quantitative comparison is under-supported in the presented table: the text claims performance similar to LiveCC, but the table mainly reports CA win-rates across training steps without a directly visible LiveCC baseline score or a full statistical comparison.

The video results rely on gist-like delimiter tokens to carry past visual information. This is an interesting workaround, but the paper does not deeply analyze how robust this compressed history is for complex multi-image/video reasoning, and D5 is acknowledged as an unresolved trade-off.

Some experimental controls could be more transparent. For the insertion baseline, sequence length, batch size, and gradient accumulation are adjusted to match token counts, but memory and optimization conditions still differ from CA training, which may confound performance comparisons.

Evaluation is broad but not exhaustive, and the paper lacks statistical significance testing across benchmarks. For a paper whose central claims concern relative performance, uncertainty estimates or repeated runs would strengthen the conclusions.

There is no explicit limitations or broader-impact discussion, although several limitations are mentioned throughout. A dedicated discussion would help contextualize when CA is preferable and when insertion remains necessary.

strengths: Provides a useful systematic decomposition (D1-D5) of the differences between cross-attention and token insertion, which helps structure the empirical comparison and identify efficiency-performance trade-offs.

The efficiency analysis and streaming live-captioning experiments convincingly illustrate CA's practical advantages: image tokens are not stored in the KV cache, enabling lower memory and latency over long horizons.
The controlled from-scratch experiments with Helium1-2B and the adaptation of Qwen2.5-VL-3B are reasonably broad, covering document/chart, OCR, general VQA, and video benchmarks.
The CA-adapted Qwen model is competitive with prior CA-based VLMs such as mPLUG-Owl3 and StreamChat on several tasks, showing that an up-to-date training pipeline narrows the previously reported gap.
The paper includes training details, public datasets, and a commitment to release code/models, which supports reproducibility.
The streaming application is a relevant and timely motivation, and the wall-time/memory measurements in Figure 4 provide concrete evidence for CA's scaling behavior.
weaknesses: The contribution is largely an empirical re-evaluation of a known idea rather than a new algorithm, theory, or dataset; the title 'CASA' does not correspond to a clearly introduced method, and the paper itself is mostly a comparison of vanilla cross-attention against token insertion.

The performance claims are overstated. The adapted Qwen CA model shows a 6.8% average drop, with much larger regressions on important tasks such as InfographicVQA (57.4 vs 77.1) and noticeable drops on ChartQA/DocVQA; video results are also 3.9% below the base model on average. This is not fully consistent with 'far more competitive' or 'retains the vast majority' without qualification.

Comparison fairness is not always convincing. The token-insertion baseline is trained with halved sequence lengths and altered batch/accumulation settings; the Qwen adaptation trains only CA layers and the last four vision blocks while comparing to a fully trained base model; and the video CA setting uses 180 frames versus 360/768 for some baselines. These choices may confound architecture effects with training or context-length effects.

The five design differences are not all systematically ablated. In particular, D5 on multi-image history is explicitly not studied, and reliance on post-image delimiter tokens as 'gist tokens' is not carefully ablated or compared with alternative visual-history mechanisms. D4 is only tested in a small-scale, frozen-encoder setting.

The live video captioning evaluation is limited: it is only against LiveCC-7B, uses an LLM-as-judge protocol, and underperforms the reported LiveCC baselines. Strong claims of practical superiority would require broader streaming benchmarks, latency/accuracy trade-off curves, and comparison to more insertion-based streaming methods.

Notation and presentation are sometimes confusing: CA^{#}, CA_{tiv}, CA_{t+v}, CAtv, and CA^{#} appear inconsistently, and the distinction between the proposed variants is not always easy to follow. The paper would benefit from clearer naming and a cleaner method section.

The experimental evidence lacks statistical rigor: no variance, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds are reported, even though many conclusions hinge on small benchmark differences. This weakens confidence in claims that CA is 'close' to token insertion.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important question: whether cross-attention (CA) can be a competitive and efficient alternative to token insertion for vision-language models, especially for long-context, multi-image, and streaming settings.

It provides a clear conceptual decomposition of cross-attention and token insertion into five design differences (D1-D5), giving a useful framework for understanding the performance-efficiency trade-offs.

The controlled experimental setting is a major strength: the authors train CA models from a text-only LLM and adapt a strong pretrained insertion-based VLM (Qwen2.5-VL-3B), comparing against insertion baselines under similar data and training pipelines.

The results credibly show that simple cross-attention is much closer to token insertion than previously reported, and can outperform prior CA-based VLMs of larger size, suggesting earlier gaps were partly due to training/data differences rather than fundamental limitations of CA.

The streaming video captioning application is compelling and demonstrates a concrete practical advantage: CA avoids image tokens in the KV cache and maintains low latency and much lower memory growth over long horizons.
The ablation studies on layer frequency, parameter sharing, token compression, and image-token FFN updates provide useful practical guidance for the community.
The paper is generally well written, with clear figures/tables and a logical structure; the Appendix provides substantial implementation and training details.
Reproducibility is supported by public training data, released models/code, and detailed hyperparameter and architectural descriptions.
The work has potential impact by encouraging renewed consideration of cross-attention in modern VLM pipelines, especially for streaming and long-context multimodal applications.
The authors appropriately acknowledge some limitations, such as remaining gaps on document/chart tasks and the memory cost of adding FFN updates.
weaknesses: The contribution is primarily an empirical re-examination rather than a fundamentally new method; experts may find the main conclusion—that CA is competitive under matched training—useful but not deeply surprising.

A substantial performance gap remains on high-resolution document, chart, and infographic tasks (e.g., InfoVQA 57.4 vs. 77.1 in the Qwen adaptation), so the claim that CA is broadly competitive with token insertion is overstated for fine-grained visual understanding.

Comparisons with prior CA-based and proprietary models are confounded by differences in training data, token budgets, base model capacity, and implementation details; reported gains over larger prior CA models do not cleanly isolate the effect of the fusion mechanism.

The streaming memory analysis is somewhat optimistic: while image tokens are excluded from the KV cache, text tokens still accumulate, so memory is not strictly constant over arbitrarily long streams.

The use of post-image delimiter tokens as gist tokens for visual history is heuristic and under-analyzed; the paper does not study how many tokens are needed, how robust this is, or how it affects long-horizon video reasoning.

Several ablations are small-scale or freeze components, and the main results appear to come from single training runs without variance or significance estimates; small reported differences may not be reliable.
The training compute (64 H100 GPUs) limits practical reproducibility despite code/model release, which is a barrier for many academic groups.

On LiveCC, the proposed 3B model reaches 39.4% win rate versus 43.2% and 41.5% for larger 7B LiveCC baselines; this is reasonable for the size, but it is not a clear streaming-performance improvement over the prior specialized system.
Some evaluation results are missing (e.g., GQA for Qwen2.5-VL, ChartQA/DocVQA for StreamChat), making cross-model comparisons less complete than ideal.
The theoretical analysis is mostly conceptual; there is no rigorous characterization of when or why cross-attention underperforms token insertion on specific task types.
